paragraphs: Neural population recordings contain many interacting signals, but low-rank recurrent networks seek a smaller set of underlying dynamics. A compact representation alone does not make those dynamics easy to interpret: different latent dimensions can remain entangled, making it difficult to assign them distinct computational roles. FacRNN adds an explicit structure to address that problem.

The framework assumes independence between groups of latent dynamics while allowing dimensions within each group to interact freely. This balances separation with flexibility: groups can evolve independently without requiring every individual dimension to represent an isolated process. The researchers formulate the recurrent model within a variational autoencoder and introduce a partial-correlation penalty that encourages separation between groups.

Experiments use synthetic data, monkey M1 recordings, and mouse voltage imaging. FacRNN consistently improves disentanglement and interpretability of both latent trajectories and low-rank connectivity compared with recurrent models lacking this independence encouragement. These findings support group-wise factorization as a useful modeling choice for making learned neural dynamics more understandable.
icml-2026-a-factorized-low-rank-rnn-fram.tldr: FacRNN encourages independence between groups of neural latent dynamics to make recurrent models of brain activity more interpretable.

paragraphs: Training a model to repair programs requires feedback about whether its edits work. Execution results provide that grounding, but they can be sparse. A reward assigned to an entire repair also leaves unclear which changed lines contributed to fixing the bug. BoostAPR addresses this credit-assignment problem by combining overall assessment with more localized feedback.

Training proceeds in three stages. First, the model learns from execution-verified repair demonstrations containing reasoning traces. Next, two reward models learn from execution outcomes: one assesses complete sequences, and the other allocates credit at the line level. Finally, PPO reinforcement learning uses the line-level model to redistribute rewards toward critical edit regions. Lines provide an intermediate unit of feedback suited to code modifications.

Trained on SWE-Gym, BoostAPR reports 40.7% on SWE-bench Verified, a 22.9-percentage-point improvement over its base model. It also reaches 24.8% on Defects4J with Python-to-Java transfer, 84.5% on HumanEval-Java, and 95.0% on QuixBugs. These results support the framework’s competitive open-source performance and its ability to generalize across languages in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-boostapr-boosting-automated-pr.tldr: BoostAPR uses execution-grounded rewards at both sequence and line levels to improve automated program repair.

paragraphs: Transferring a predictor from a labeled graph to an unlabeled graph creates two linked challenges: adapting to a different domain and maintaining fairness. Existing approaches often depend on sensitive-attribute information from the target domain, which may be unavailable. CELL addresses this setting without requiring target sensitive labels.

CELL uses a causal graph to describe how graph data are generated and to guide representation learning. Separate encoders extract sensitive factors and causal factors. A conditional mutual-information objective encourages these representations to separate, reducing their remaining dependence under the conditioning used by the method. To use unlabeled target data, CELL generates estimated task labels and sensitive attributes, then uses similarity relationships to derive node representations intended to reduce bias.

A fairness-aware bipartite graph supplies additional structural supervision for aligning the two domains. This combines factor separation with information about relationships across graphs. Benchmark experiments show consistent improvements over strong baselines in both prediction and fairness. The results support treating fairness and domain alignment together, including when actual sensitive labels are unavailable in the target graph.
icml-2026-cell-a-causal-perspective-for-.tldr: CELL combines causal factor separation and graph alignment to improve prediction and fairness without target-domain sensitive labels.

paragraphs: Federated continual learning lets distributed devices learn successive tasks over time. Assuming that every device reaches a new task simultaneously can leave faster clients waiting. Allowing asynchronous progress avoids that synchronization requirement, but the server then receives updates from different tasks and stages of learning. Their interference can corrupt the shared model.

C²-AFCL addresses this task drift through two stages of calibration. The first uses task-aware caches to reduce variation caused by local client drift. The second estimates an interference subspace from historical task knowledge. It then uses orthogonal projection to remove conflicting components from new updates, aiming to retain earlier knowledge while incorporating new tasks.

The approach therefore considers the semantic conflict between updates, alongside differences arising within individual clients. Experiments show significant improvements over existing methods and demonstrate robust, efficient learning in dynamic federated environments. The findings support calibrating updates according to their relationship with previously learned tasks when devices progress at different rates, rather than requiring clients to share a synchronized task schedule.
icml-2026-cross-task-calibration-for-asy.tldr: C²-AFCL reduces interference between asynchronous client updates so a federated model can learn new tasks while preserving earlier knowledge.

paragraphs: Continual release involves publishing updated answers as data arrive while maintaining differential privacy. This paper studies tasks involving maximum or minimum cumulative sums and the selection of attributes associated with those sums. Earlier results establish that these tasks must incur substantial error when accuracy is measured using a purely additive allowance.

The paper changes the accuracy formulation by permitting a relative-error term, so part of the allowed discrepancy scales with the quantity being measured. Under non-adaptively generated input streams, this substantially reduces the error that algorithms need to allow. The result depends on how the stream is generated; it is not a blanket improvement for all possible sequences of incoming records.

When records can instead be chosen adaptively, the authors prove that selecting an attribute with a small cumulative sum still requires large error. Other studied tasks retain achievable small-error bounds. Nearly matching lower bounds complement the algorithms. Together, these results identify a meaningful separation between adaptive and non-adaptive streams and show where relative-error guarantees can overcome purely additive barriers.
icml-2026-differentially-private-continu.tldr: Allowing relative error improves private continual-release guarantees for non-adaptive streams, while adaptive streams retain a sharp obstacle for minimum selection.

paragraphs: Persona-based jailbreaks try to change a language model’s safety behavior through the role or character it is asked to adopt. This paper argues that defenses need a systematic way to keep safety decisions separate from that persona context. Persona-Invariant Alignment, or PIA, trains attacks and defenses together through adversarial self-play.

The attack component, Persona Lineage Evolution, explores risky personas and propagates credit through their lineages. The defense component, Persona-Invariant Consistency Learning, uses a one-sided KL-divergence constraint to encourage the separation of safety decisions from persona context. Its theoretical grounding rests on a structural separation hypothesis. That hypothesis is part of the framework’s foundation, rather than an unconditional claim that role and safety can always be separated.

Experiments show that the attack component efficiently explores high-risk persona spaces. The defense significantly lowers attack success while preserving general model capability. These findings support the proposed combination of evolving attacks and consistency-based defense as a way to improve resistance to persona manipulation in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-disentangling-intent-from-role.tldr: PIA uses adversarial self-play and consistency learning to reduce persona-based jailbreak success while preserving general model capability.

paragraphs: A language model can score well on benchmarks yet fail to deliver what a person actually wanted from an interaction. This paper studies that gap through real user expectations. It argues that evaluations based on expert rubrics, model heuristics, or simulated users miss some of the diversity and subtlety of human needs.

The researchers develop a principled procedure for extracting expectations with rich semantic content and use it to build ExpectBench. Grounding the benchmark in real interactions makes user expectations a direct object of evaluation. Their analyses find that current models struggle both to satisfy those expectations and to anticipate what users hope to receive.

The paper then introduces LENS, a lightweight response-generation framework that explicitly models latent expectations. Its purpose is to help a model internalize the expectations behind an interaction and produce a better-aligned answer. The reported improvements in expectation satisfaction are consistent across the study’s evaluations. This supports explicit expectation modeling as a useful direction for making language-model assistance better reflect real user needs.
icml-2026-expectation-alignment-of-langu.tldr: ExpectBench measures real user expectations, and LENS improves response alignment by explicitly modeling those expectations.

paragraphs: Text can describe events that change a time series, but it usually expresses their effects qualitatively or indirectly. Forecasting models need numerical signals. This mismatch makes it difficult to combine the two effectively. Controlled semi-synthetic experiments in this paper find that existing methods focus too much on redundant tokens and struggle to convert textual meaning into useful numerical cues.

TESS introduces an intermediate representation called the Temporal Evolution Semantic Space. A language model uses structured prompting to extract four interpretable kinds of temporal information: distribution shift, volatility, shape, and lag. These numerically grounded primitives provide a more explicit connection between an event description and its potential time-series effects. Confidence-aware gating filters the extracted information before it is used.

Across four real-world datasets, the method reduces forecasting error by up to 29% against state-of-the-art unimodal and multimodal baselines. That figure is the largest reported reduction, not a uniform gain across datasets. The findings support translating text into structured temporal signals as an effective way to bridge the forecasting modality gap.
icml-2026-from-text-to-forecasts-bridgin.tldr: TESS translates text into interpretable temporal signals, improving forecasting error by up to 29% in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Supervised graph outlier detection often has far fewer anomalous examples than normal ones. Generating additional outliers can help address that imbalance, but diffusion-based generation requires repeated sampling steps and introduces stochastic variation. GOCM proposes a consistency-model approach that synthesizes graph outliers in a single step.

Its Origin Consistency mechanism uses an interval-based inference strategy to derive a direct mapping from a noise trajectory to the data origin. The framework also handles graphs containing multiple kinds of relationships through a Multi-input Variational Graph Auto-Encoder. This component processes relations separately, combines information across them, and maps the resulting structure into a shared latent space. GOCM generates outlier nodes from that representation.

Experiments on multiple real-world datasets report superior detection performance together with significantly better generation efficiency. The contribution combines a faster synthesis mechanism with a representation designed for heterogeneous graph structure. The findings indicate that reducing generation to one step can still produce useful synthetic outliers, improving the downstream detection task while reducing the computational burden of augmentation.
icml-2026-gocm-single-step-graph-outlier.tldr: GOCM synthesizes graph outliers in one step, improving generation efficiency and downstream detection in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Many kinds of data contain relationships that can be represented as graphs. Yet learning systems often construct graph representations for one task or modality and then discard them. This paper asks how those structures could persist across learning contexts, allowing recurring relational patterns to accumulate in a shared representation.

G-Substrate implements that idea with two complementary mechanisms. A unified structural schema makes graph representations compatible across different modalities and tasks. An interleaved, role-based training strategy then exposes the same graph structure to multiple functions during learning. Compatibility supplies a common representational form, while varied training roles give that shared structure opportunities to be useful in different contexts.

Experiments span multiple domains, modalities, and tasks. G-Substrate outperforms both task-isolated approaches and naive multi-task learning methods. These findings support organizing learning around reusable intermediate graph structures, beyond simply training several tasks together. The paper’s central contribution is therefore a way to preserve and develop relational representations across contexts where graph structure would otherwise be repeatedly reconstructed.
icml-2026-graph-is-a-substrate-across-da.tldr: G-Substrate uses a shared graph schema and varied training roles to accumulate reusable structure across modalities and tasks.

paragraphs: Diverse post-training data can improve a language model’s downstream performance, but linguistic variety is only a weak indicator of task-relevant variety. Two collections may differ substantially in wording without covering the features that matter to the model. This paper measures diversity in an interpretable feature space through Feature Activation Coverage, or FAC.

FAC Synthesis turns that measure into a data-generation procedure. It uses a sparse autoencoder to identify features missing from an initial dataset, then generates samples that explicitly express those features. The objective is to fill representational gaps in the seed data. This connects the choice of new examples to the model’s feature coverage rather than relying solely on surface differences between texts.

Experiments report consistent improvements in both diversity and downstream performance across instruction following, toxicity detection, reward modeling, and behavior steering. The researchers also identify a shared interpretable feature space across LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen, enabling cross-model knowledge transfer. These findings support feature coverage as a practical guide for targeted synthetic-data construction.
icml-2026-less-is-enough-synthesizing-di.tldr: FAC Synthesis generates examples that fill missing interpretable features, improving data diversity and downstream language-model performance.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based graph solvers repeatedly evaluate large sets of interactions while searching for combinatorial solutions. That repeated work can make inference slow and exhaust memory on larger problems. LoRe is a training-free wrapper that limits the fraction of interactions evaluated at each iteration.

The selected interactions change during inference. LoRe directs computation toward those with high conflict or uncertainty, rather than retaining a fixed sparse graph or mask throughout the process. This makes the interaction budget adaptive to the solver’s current state. The approach draws inspiration from computational methods in many-body physics and can be applied at inference time without retraining the underlying solver.

On Maximum Independent Set, LoRe extends feasible inference more than threefold beyond the baseline’s out-of-memory limit, with approximately eightfold speedup and twelvefold lower peak memory while preserving solution quality in that regime. On Traveling Salesperson problems with 1,000 nodes, it reports approximately fifteenfold speedup and forty-fourfold memory reduction with competitive tours. The study also reports zero-shot robustness to topology shifts, supporting usefulness across the tested tasks and graph structures.
icml-2026-lore-adaptive-interaction-eval.tldr: LoRe dynamically budgets graph interactions during inference, substantially reducing runtime and memory use while retaining strong solution quality.

paragraphs: Rotary position embeddings help Transformers represent where inputs are located, but extending them to multidimensional data raises geometric questions. Existing extensions often rotate each axis independently or mix frequencies empirically. According to this paper, those choices limit interactions across dimensions and can make representations behave differently depending on direction.

nD-RoPE develops a unified formulation for arbitrary dimensions without decomposing positions into independent axes. Starting from a translation-invariant formulation in a continuous Hilbert space, the authors derive a spectral condition for isotropy, meaning balanced behavior across directions. This condition requires treating positions and frequencies as coupled multidimensional vectors.

The practical construction uses regular-simplex wave vectors at multiple scales. It provides non-degenerate spatial coverage and a symmetric, directionally balanced second-order response. That specific property should not be broadened into a claim of perfect directional invariance in every respect. Experiments on images, videos, and point clouds show consistent performance gains and improved generalization, supporting the value of a geometrically grounded approach to multidimensional positional representation.
icml-2026-nd-rope-a-generalized-rope-for.tldr: nD-RoPE generalizes rotary position embeddings through coupled multidimensional geometry and improves performance across images, videos, and point clouds.

paragraphs: Neural simulators can approximate physical dynamics, but a single end-to-end network may lose some of the interpretability and reliability associated with traditional numerical methods. Neural Modular Physics addresses elastic simulation by organizing learned computation into physically meaningful modules. The design follows the modular organization of classical simulators.

These neural modules communicate through intermediate physical quantities. That structure allows training to supervise intermediate values directly and impose physical constraints within the computational flow. A specialized architecture and training strategy turn the numerical workflow into a modular neural simulator. The approach combines learned approximation with explicit physical organization, making the internal computation more accessible to supervision.

Experiments show better generalization to unseen initial conditions and resolutions, stable long-horizon simulation, and stronger preservation of physical properties than other neural simulators. The paper also reports greater feasibility than traditional simulators when underlying dynamics are unknown. These findings support physical modularity as a useful design principle for learned elastic simulation, with benefits spanning generalization, stability, and the handling of incompletely specified dynamics.
icml-2026-neural-modular-physics-for-ela.tldr: Neural Modular Physics organizes elastic simulation into physically meaningful learned modules to improve consistency, stability, and generalization.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary object detectors need to recognize novel categories and locate their objects accurately. Existing methods transfer knowledge from CLIP into regional features, but using those same features for classification and localization can improve semantic alignment at the expense of spatial precision. OSSD separates these two learning objectives.

The first stage transfers object-level semantic information from CLIP’s global classification embeddings to improve discrimination between regions. The second transfers fine-grained spatial and structural information from a detector trained only on COCO base categories. This gives semantic and spatial learning distinct sources of supervision. An additional Location Quality Estimation Head predicts localization quality independently of object category, complementing confidence that a region contains an object.

The method reaches 49.2 AP50 on OV-COCO and 40.5 mAP for novel categories on OV-LVIS, exceeding previous best results as reported in the abstract. These findings support explicitly separating what an object is from how well it has been localized. They also show the usefulness of supplementing objectness confidence with a dedicated estimate of location quality.
icml-2026-object-level-semantic-and-spat.tldr: OSSD separates semantic and spatial knowledge transfer to improve recognition and localization of novel object categories.

paragraphs: LiDAR-based object detectors are central to autonomous driving, making missed objects a serious robustness concern. Existing attacks that perturb individual points often fail to make an entire object disappear from detection and can be difficult to realize physically. OBJVanish studies adversarial objects whose generated three-dimensional forms can be implemented in physical settings.

An initial empirical investigation identifies compositions of multiple objects as the dominant factor in the studied detection vulnerabilities. The framework then uses prompt-driven text-to-3D generation to construct pedestrian instances under physical constraints. It limits generation to valid combinations drawn from a curated pool of representative real-world 3D models. This constraint connects the generated cases to realizable objects.

Experiments report consistent evasion of six state-of-the-art LiDAR detectors in simulation and real-world physical settings. Here, invisibility refers to missed detection by the object detectors, rather than a claim that the objects produce no LiDAR signal. The results expose vulnerabilities associated with physically realizable object compositions and demonstrate their relevance beyond point-level perturbations tested only in simulation.
icml-2026-objvanish-prompt-driven-genera.tldr: OBJVanish generates physically realizable object compositions that evade LiDAR object detectors in simulated and real-world evaluations.

paragraphs: Larger visual autoregressive models can generate better outputs, but their inference costs grow. Mixture-of-experts architectures offer sparse activation, using only part of the model’s parameters for a given computation. Prism-MoE investigates how to obtain that benefit by converting an existing dense visual generator, avoiding the expense of training an expert-based model from scratch.

The conversion has two main components. Trajectory-consistent initialization treats expert initialization as a decomposition problem and preserves the pretrained model’s generation trajectory. Confidence-adaptive sparse fine-tuning then guides expert specialization using routing supervision informed by confidence. This connects the assignment of visual tokens to experts with the information density of those tokens.

Experiments achieve conversion with less than 10% of the standard training budget. The resulting models maintain generation quality comparable to dense baselines while using only 37.5% active parameters. Those figures describe training cost and active model capacity, respectively. Together, they support dense-to-MoE conversion as a practical way to retain pretrained visual generation quality while shifting computation toward sparse expert activation.
icml-2026-prism-moe-efficient-dense-to-m.tldr: Prism-MoE converts dense visual generators into sparse expert models with under 10% of the standard training budget and comparable generation quality.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis works backward from a desired product molecule to possible reactants. The paper argues that static pattern-matching methods limit logical decision-making and make their predictions difficult to interpret. Retro-Expert combines language models with specialized chemical models to generate both reactant predictions and explanations grounded in chemical logic.

The framework divides the work into three connected components. Specialized models supply chemical knowledge, which is distilled into a decision space for the reasoning process. A language model performs critical reasoning within that space, producing a prediction together with an interpretable path. Knowledge-grounded policy optimization then refines the decision policy through reinforcement learning. This arrangement brings specialized chemical information into the language model’s reasoning process.

Experiments show that Retro-Expert surpasses both language-model-based approaches and specialized models across the evaluated metrics. It also produces chemically grounded explanations that the paper reports as enhancing chemists’ trust in practice. The findings support collaborative reasoning as a way to improve predictive performance while exposing the chemical logic behind proposed reactants.
icml-2026-retro-expert-collaborative-rea.tldr: Retro-Expert combines specialized chemical models and language-model reasoning to improve retrosynthesis predictions and provide chemically grounded explanations.

paragraphs: Evaluating robot manipulation policies in the real world is expensive. Learned world models offer an alternative, but their predicted videos can hide failures by making them appear successful or produce artifacts under unfamiliar controls. Such behavior undermines policy evaluation even when the generated scenes look plausible.

dWorldEval gives actions a central role in its discrete-diffusion architecture. Visual observations, language instructions, and action chunks enter a shared token space and are processed by one self-attention backbone. Actions therefore participate as first-class tokens. A sparse keyframe memory anchors the overall scene state while retaining detailed interaction cues across views. Progress-as-text jointly generates future observations and indicators of success.

Experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and real-robot tasks show significantly better action controllability than video-diffusion baselines. The model also stabilizes long-horizon, multi-view rollouts and supports accurate policy ranking through automatic success estimation. These results connect world-model quality to its intended evaluation role: predictions need to reflect the consequences of robot actions well enough to distinguish stronger policies from weaker ones.
icml-2026-scaling-robot-policy-evaluatio.tldr: dWorldEval centers actions in a discrete-diffusion world model to produce more reliable simulated robot-policy evaluations.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by having a lightweight draft model propose several tokens that a larger model verifies in parallel. Its practical adoption depends on good draft models and the infrastructure needed to train them. SpecForge addresses both needs with an open-source training framework and a released collection of trained drafts.

The framework fully supports EAGLE-3 and combines target–draft decoupling, hybrid parallelism, optimized training kernels, and integration with production inference engines. These changes target the training workflow as a whole. For Qwen3-235B-A22B, the reported EAGLE-3 training speedup reaches 9.9 times the baseline.

The accompanying SpecBundle provides EAGLE-3 draft models for mainstream open-source language models. On SGLang, these drafts achieve up to 4.48-fold end-to-end inference speedup. The training and inference figures concern different stages, and both are reported maxima. A systematic study also yields practical training recipes. Together, the framework, draft releases, and recipes aim to make speculative decoding easier to adopt and less costly to prepare for deployment.
icml-2026-specforge-a-flexible-and-effic.tldr: SpecForge accelerates speculative-decoding training and releases draft models that deliver up to 4.48-fold end-to-end inference speedup.

paragraphs: Tool-using language models can solve complex tasks efficiently, but their tool-calling behavior introduces a distinct vulnerability. Sponge Tool Attack studies whether a rewritten prompt can make an otherwise efficient agent consume substantially more computation while still pursuing the same task. The target is the efficiency of the reasoning process.

The attack operates under a strict query-only assumption: it changes the input prompt without modifying the model or its tools. An iterative, multi-agent framework produces benign-looking rewrites with high semantic fidelity and explicit policy control. These prompts turn concise reasoning trajectories into unnecessarily lengthy and complicated ones before the final answer, preserving the original task meaning and user intent.

Experiments cover six models, twelve tools, four agentic frameworks, and thirteen datasets across five domains, including open-source models and closed-source APIs. The reported findings validate the attack’s effectiveness across that tested range. The study shows that preserving the apparent task and eventual answer can coexist with substantial computational overhead, making execution efficiency a meaningful dimension of agent robustness.
icml-2026-sponge-tool-attack-stealthy-de.tldr: Sponge Tool Attack rewrites prompts to inflate tool-using agents’ computation while preserving the original task’s meaning.

paragraphs: Contrastive representation learning is widely used, but its theoretical relationship to retrieval quality has remained incomplete. Earlier generalization bounds can also worsen as the number of negative samples grows, despite observed benefits from larger negative sets. This paper develops a statistical framework connecting contrastive training, generalization, and downstream ranking.

For retrieval, the authors use an AUC-type population criterion and show that contrastive loss is statistically consistent with optimal ranking. A calibration-style inequality quantifies how excess contrastive risk relates to excess retrieval suboptimality. This supplies a formal connection between improving the training objective and approaching better retrieval rankings within the analysis.

For supervised contrastive learning, the generalization bound has order O(1/m + 1/√n); for self-supervised learning, it has order O(1/√m + 1/√n). Here, m counts negatives and n counts anchor points. Both bounds improve with more negatives while retaining a separate dependence on anchors, exposing a trade-off between the two. Experiments with large-scale vision–language models corroborate the theoretical predictions, connecting the analysis to observed model behavior.
icml-2026-statistical-consistency-and-ge.tldr: The paper links contrastive loss to optimal retrieval ranking and derives generalization bounds that improve with larger negative sets.

paragraphs: Robot planners based on predicted video can describe plausible futures, but operating on two-dimensional frames can leave them without the geometric understanding needed for precise spatial reasoning. This paper proposes predicting how a scene’s three-dimensional structure evolves over time. That combination of spatial structure and temporal evolution motivates the model’s four-dimensional representation.

The model predicts within a structured latent space, conditioned on observations and textual instructions. Its representation captures the scene holistically and can be decoded into multiple three-dimensional formats. To use these predictions for control, a goal-conditioned inverse dynamics module converts generated future scenes into executable robot actions. Scene prediction and action generation thus form a complete planning pipeline.

Experiments show strong visual quality and substantially better three-dimensional consistency and agreement across views than state-of-the-art video-based planners. The full system also achieves superior performance on complex manipulation tasks, generalizes robustly to novel visual conditions, and works on real robotic platforms. These findings support explicit evolving scene geometry as a useful foundation for robot planning.
icml-2026-structured-4d-latent-predictiv.tldr: The model plans robot actions by predicting evolving 3D scenes, improving geometric consistency and manipulation performance.

paragraphs: Identifiable virtual faces aim to protect a person’s original appearance while remaining usable for identity recognition. A virtual face should differ visually and statistically from the original, yet still support that recognition function. TIVDiff addresses additional challenges in this setting: image quality, control over facial presentation, and verification that a generated face is legitimate.

The diffusion framework learns a virtual identity space through Virtual Identity Projection. It then conditions face generation on that virtual identity and three-dimensional facial geometry, preserving pose and expression. This separates the identity representation used for synthesis from the geometric information needed to maintain the face’s presentation.

For legitimacy verification, Identity-Guarded Generative Watermarking links the diffusion process’s initial noise to the virtual identity through a reversible mapping. This embeds an imperceptible verification cue in the generated face. Experiments report advantages over state-of-the-art virtual-face schemes in image quality, identifiability, and trustworthiness. The contribution combines recognizable virtual identities with a built-in verification mechanism, addressing both the usefulness of the generated face and the ability to check its legitimacy.
icml-2026-towards-trustworthy-and-identi.tldr: TIVDiff generates identifiable virtual faces with preserved pose and expression and an imperceptible cue for legitimacy verification.

paragraphs: Foundation models increasingly need useful estimates of uncertainty, but applying Bayesian methods throughout very large networks can be computationally expensive. Variational Mixture-of-Experts Routing, or VMoER, concentrates Bayesian inference on the decision about which experts to activate. This targets a limited part of an architecture already designed around sparse computation.

The framework replaces the usual deterministic treatment of expert selection with structured uncertainty modeling. The authors implement two approaches: amortized variational inference over routing logits, and inference of a temperature parameter governing stochastic expert selection. Both place uncertainty in routing rather than requiring Bayesian inference across every model parameter.

Across the tested foundation models, VMoER improves routing stability under noise by 38%, reduces calibration error by 94%, and increases out-of-distribution AUROC by 12%, with less than 1% additional FLOPs. These results combine stronger uncertainty-related behavior with a small computational increment. They suggest that Bayesian expert selection offers a scalable route toward better-calibrated foundation models, with the reported benefits grounded in the models and conditions evaluated.
icml-2026-variational-routing-a-scalable.tldr: VMoER confines Bayesian uncertainty modeling to expert routing, improving calibration and robustness with less than 1% additional FLOPs.
